title: Your LLM Judge Is a Confident Liar: Building Better Verifiers — Browserbase
talk_summary: Browserbase and Microsoft researchers show that off-the-shelf LLM judges (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o) are confidently wrong, inflating a web agent's success from ~38% true to 74% judged. They build a 'universal verifier' that generates a task-specific rubric, retrieves only the top-K relevant evidence screenshots per criterion, isolates criteria so errors don't cascade, and separates controllable from uncontrollable failures, reaching human-level inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa 0.58) and cutting false positives from ~half to zero.

takeaways.technique: Rubric-based verifier with per-criterion evidence retrieval
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of one holistic pass/fail judgment, they first generate a ~10-criterion rubric of what success looks like for the specific task, then for each criterion rank and pull only the top-K most relevant evidence (screenshots/trajectory) before deciding that criterion.
takeaways.numbers: false positives reduced from almost half to zero; Cohen's kappa 0.58 vs human annotators

takeaways.technique: Isolate rubric criteria to prevent error cascade
takeaways.what_they_do: Each rubric criterion is graded independently so a mistake in one step doesn't poison downstream criteria; they explicitly penalize only the criterion where the error occurred.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we also did not want errors to cascade from one rubric uh criterion to another. We wanted them to be isolated

takeaways.technique: Grade only what was asked; no extraneous criteria
takeaways.what_they_do: Rubrics must not add requirements the task didn't ask for, because naive rubric generation invents extra criteria that artificially deflate scores.
takeaways.evidence_quote: This is actually an extraneous criterion that was not asked for in the task but we saw a lot of rubrics naively generated do something like this

takeaways.what_they_do: They enumerate failure modes and assign credit differently when the agent did its best but the environment blocked it (e.g., item out of stock) versus when the agent made a controllable mistake or hallucinated.

takeaways.technique: Validate the verifier against held-out human labels (Cohen's kappa)
takeaways.what_they_do: They built a platform to collect human ground-truth labels with 2x overlap, held out two-thirds of labels from iteration, and measured verifier-vs-human agreement with Cohen's kappa, treating human inter-annotator agreement as the ceiling.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we held out at least twothirds of the labels. Um like we did not train like iterate on them
takeaways.numbers: 0.58 Cohen's kappa; verifier agrees with humans as often as humans agree with each other

takeaways.technique: Auto-research loop to build/tune verifiers, human-primed
takeaways.what_they_do: They ran an auto-research loop that iterated on the verifier prompts/code, running ~30 experiments in a day; it reached ~70% of human-built agreement alone, but primed with human findings it exceeded the manual result.
takeaways.evidence_quote: an auto research loop could do it in about one day. It ran the same number of experiments in about one day. However, it only reached about 70%
takeaways.numbers: 3 weeks manual vs ~1 day auto; auto alone ~70% of manual agreement; primed auto exceeded manual
